setup.title: How Exam P works & how to study

sections.title: What Exam P actually tests
sections.body:
Exam P is a 3-hour, 30-question multiple-choice CBT. Weights are roughly:

• General Probability 23–30%
• Univariate random variables 44–50% (biggest)
• Multivariate 23–30%

You are not tested on measure theory, coding, or advanced finance. You are tested on whether you can set up a probability model quickly and compute cleanly under time pressure.

sections.title: How this app forces good study
sections.body:
Each day has two gates:

1) Learn session — concept, worked examples, and why the method works
2) Quiz — about 20 exam-style MC questions

You cannot start the quiz until the learn session is finished (sections + concept checks). Wrong quiz answers go to a Wrong Pool and come back later.

sections.title: Example of the right exam mindset
sections.setup: A problem mentions “ordinary deductible of 100” and asks for the insurer’s expected payment.
sections.solution: Do not jump into calculus blindly. First define X = loss, then payment Y = max(X−100, 0) or (X−100)+. Then compute E[Y] with the correct distribution of X.
sections.why: Exam P rewards clean definitions. Most errors are wrong random variable, not hard math.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Which topic cluster carries the largest syllabus weight on Exam P?
sections.explain: Univariate RVs are 44–50% of the exam — plan most practice there.

sections.title: Sample space and events
sections.body:
A random experiment has a sample space S (all possible outcomes).

An event A is a subset of S. Probability is a function P(·) on events with axioms:

1) P(A) ≥ 0
2) P(S) = 1
3) If A and B are disjoint (A∩B=∅), then P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)

From these you get P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A) and inclusion-exclusion.

sections.title: Unions, intersections, complements
sections.body:
A∪B: A or B or both
A∩B: both
Aᶜ: not A

Inclusion-exclusion (2 sets):
P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)

For 3 sets, expand carefully with all pairwise intersections and the triple intersection.

sections.title: Worked: none of three sports
sections.why: We convert “none” into the complement of the union. Complements are almost always easier than listing every outside region.

sections.title: Worked: both lab and referral
sections.setup: P(neither lab nor referral)=0.35, P(referral)=0.30, P(lab)=0.40. Find P(both).
sections.why: Inclusion-exclusion rearranges to isolate the intersection when the union is known via a complement statement.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: If A and B are disjoint, which is always true?
sections.explain: Disjoint ⇒ intersection empty ⇒ probabilities add. Independence is the product rule, which is different.

sections.title: When order matters
sections.body:
Fundamental counting: if stage 1 has n1 options, stage 2 has n2, … total = n1·n2·…

Permutations (order matters):
P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)!

Combinations (order does not matter):
C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!)

Classic rule: if the problem says “committee”, “hand of cards”, “choose a set”, use C. If it says “rank”, “assign distinct roles”, “password order”, use P.

sections.title: Worked: urn / same color balls
sections.setup: Urn1: 4 red, 6 blue. Urn2: 16 red, x blue. One ball from each. P(same color)=0.44. Find x.
sections.solution:
P(same)=Pboth red + Pboth blue.
(4/10)(16/(16+x)) + (6/10)(x/(16+x))=0.44.
Solve → x=4.
sections.why: We multiply across independent draws, then add mutually exclusive color cases. Counting denominators is just sizes of urns.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Number of 5-card hands from 52 cards uses:
sections.explain: A hand is an unordered set of cards → combinations.

sections.title: With/without replacement & identical objects
sections.body:
Without replacement: denominators shrink (hypergeometric-style counting).
With replacement / independent trials: denominators stay fixed.

Multinomial coefficient for splitting n distinct into groups of sizes n1,...,nk:
 n!/(n1! ... nk!).

If objects are identical within type, count distinct sequences carefully — do not overcount.

sections.title: Worked: committee with roles vs without
sections.setup: 10 people. (a) Choose 3 for a committee. (b) Choose president, secretary, treasurer (distinct).
sections.why: Same people, different whether order/roles matter. Misreading this is the #1 counting trap.

sections.title: Order check
sections.prompt: Passwords of length 4 from 10 distinct chars, no repeat — use:
sections.explain: Order matters and no repeats ⇒ permutation P(10,4).

sections.title: Building probabilities from axioms
sections.body:
Useful identities:
• P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A)
• If A⊂B then P(A)≤P(B)
• P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)
• P(A∪B∪C) expanded form for 3 sets

Classical model (equally likely outcomes):
P(A)=# favorable / # possible
Only use this when outcomes truly are equally likely.

sections.title: Worked: complement shortcut
sections.setup: P(A∪B)=0.7 and P(A∪Bᶜ)=0.9. Find P(A).
sections.solution:
Note B and Bᶜ partition. A = (A∩B)∪(A∩Bᶜ).
Also P(A∪B)+P(A∪Bᶜ)=P(A)+1 ⇒ 0.7+0.9=P(A)+1 ⇒ P(A)=0.6.
sections.why: Adding those two unions double-counts A and covers the whole space once for B∪Bᶜ. Algebra isolates P(A) without drawing a complicated Venn by hand.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: P(Aᶜ) equals:
sections.explain: Axiom consequence: A and Aᶜ partition S.

sections.title: Boole / Bonferroni and partitions
sections.body:
If A1,...,An are a partition of S (disjoint, union S), then P(B)=Σ P(B∩Ai).

Boole's inequality: P(∪Ai) ≤ Σ P(Ai).
Lower bound sometimes: P(∪Ai) ≥ max P(Ai).

Exam habit: rewrite messy 'at least one' as complement of 'none', and rewrite 'exactly one' as mutually exclusive pieces.

sections.title: Worked: exactly one of two events
sections.setup: P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A∩B)=0.2. Find P(exactly one of A,B).
sections.why: Inclusion-exclusion for the symmetric difference. Draw a Venn if the algebra feels slippery.

sections.title: Complement habit
sections.prompt: P(at least one of A,B) is best rewritten as:
sections.explain: At least one is the complement of none (neither).

sections.title: Definition and multiplication rule
sections.body:
Conditional probability:
P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B)   (when P(B)>0)

Multiplication rule (rearranged):
P(A∩B)=P(B)·P(A|B)=P(A)·P(B|A)

Tree diagrams are the exam-friendly way to organize multi-stage experiments.

sections.title: Worked: heart disease given parents
sections.setup: 937 men; 210 heart deaths; 312 had a parent with heart disease, and 102 of those 312 died of heart disease. Find P(heart death | no parent heart disease).
sections.solution:
No-parent group size: 937−312=625.
Heart deaths in that group: 210−102=108.
Conditional prob: 108/625=0.1728 ≈ 0.173.
sections.why: “Given that” means restrict the denominator to the conditioning set. Count carefully inside that restricted world only.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: P(A∩B) always equals:
sections.explain: Multiplication rule. Product P(A)P(B) only if independent.

sections.title: Law of total probability
sections.body:
If B1,…,Bk partition S (disjoint, cover all), then
P(A)=Σ P(A|Bi)P(Bi)

Think: break the world into risk classes / machine types / disease states, then average.

sections.title: Bayes’ theorem
sections.body:
P(Bi|A)=P(A|Bi)P(Bi) / Σ P(A|Bj)P(Bj)

In words:
posterior ∝ likelihood × prior

Exam language: “given a positive test”, “given a claim occurred”, “given the ball is red” — reverse the conditioning.

sections.title: Worked: Bayes template
sections.setup: 2% of policies are high-risk. High-risk claim rate 30%, low-risk 5%. A random policy has a claim. P(high-risk | claim)?
sections.why: Claims are more common from low-risk simply because there are many more of them. Bayes reweights priors by likelihoods; intuition without the formula often fails.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Bayes is mainly used to:
sections.explain: We start with P(data|class) and want P(class|data).

sections.title: Two different ideas people confuse
sections.body:
Mutually exclusive (disjoint): A∩B=∅ ⇒ P(A∩B)=0. They cannot happen together.

Independent: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), or equivalently P(A|B)=P(A).
Knowing B happened does not change A.

If A and B both have positive probability, they cannot be both independent and mutually exclusive (except trivial cases).

sections.title: Worked: independent coverages
sections.setup: P(collision)=2 P(disability), independent, P(both)=0.15. Find P(neither).
sections.why: Independence supplies the product for the intersection, which lets us solve for the unknown probabilities.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: If A and B are independent with P(A),P(B)>0, then A and B:
sections.explain: Independence implies P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)>0, so not disjoint.

uni_discrete_def.title: Discrete RVs: PMF, CDF, E, Var

sections.title: What a discrete random variable is
sections.body:
A random variable X maps outcomes to numbers.

Discrete: X takes countable values x1,x2,…

PMF: p(x)=P(X=x), with p(x)≥0 and Σ p(x)=1.

CDF: F(x)=P(X≤x)=Σ_{t≤x} p(t).

Always state the support (possible values) before computing.

sections.title: Expectation and variance
sections.body:
E[X]=Σ x p(x)
E[g(X)]=Σ g(x) p(x)   (law of the unconscious statistician)
Var(X)=E[X²]−(E[X])² = E[(X−μ)²]
SD=√Var
CV=SD/|mean| when mean≠0

Linearity always works: E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b
Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X)

sections.title: Worked: E and Var from a PMF table
sections.why: Variance needs the second moment. Computing E[X²] then subtracting μ² is faster and less error-prone than expanding (x−μ)² for every point.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Var(X) equals:
sections.explain: Standard computational formula for variance.

sections.title: Binomial
sections.body:
X~Binomial(n,p): number of successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials.

P(X=k)=C(n,k) p^k (1−p)^{n−k}, k=0,…,n
E[X]=np, Var(X)=np(1−p)

Use when: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independence.

sections.title: Poisson
sections.body:
X~Poisson(λ): counts of rare events in a continuum of exposure.

P(X=k)=e^{−λ} λ^k / k!, k=0,1,2,…
E[X]=Var(X)=λ

If independent Xi~Poisson(λi), sum is Poisson(Σλi).
Binomial(n,p) with n large, p small, np=λ is approximately Poisson(λ).

sections.title: Worked: choose the model
sections.setup: An insurer has 1000 independent policies, each has 1% claim chance. Approximate P(exactly 8 claims).
sections.solution:
Exact: Binomial(1000,0.01). Approx: Poisson(λ=10).
P(X=8)≈ e^{−10} 10^8 / 8!.
sections.why: n large, p small, np moderate → Poisson approximation reduces calculation while matching the exam’s modeling intent.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: For X~Poisson(λ), which is true?
sections.explain: Equal mean and variance is the Poisson signature.

sections.title: Read the definition of X carefully
sections.body:
Geometric: usually “trials until first success” OR “failures before first success”. Formulas change — match the book/exam wording.

Negative binomial: trials until r successes (or failures before r successes).

Hypergeometric: draws without replacement from a finite population with K successes in N items; X=#successes in n draws.

Use hypergeometric when dependence from finite sampling matters; binomial when with replacement / large population.

sections.title: Worked: hypergeometric vs binomial
sections.setup: Urn has 5 defective in 20. Draw 4 without replacement. P(exactly 1 defective)?
sections.why: Without replacement changes the probabilities each draw, so independent Bernoulli trials (binomial) would be wrong.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Sampling without replacement from a finite dichotomous population is modeled by:
sections.explain: Hypergeometric is the without-replacement count model.

sections.title: PDF and CDF
sections.body:
Continuous X has PDF f with f(x)≥0 and ∫ f=1.

P(a≤X≤b)=∫_a^b f(x)dx
(note P(X=exact point)=0)

CDF F(x)=P(X≤x)=∫_{−∞}^x f
Then f=F′ when F is differentiable.

Percentile π_p: F(π_p)=p.

sections.title: Uniform(a,b)
sections.body:
f(x)=1/(b−a) on [a,b]
E[X]=(a+b)/2
Var(X)=(b−a)²/12

Probabilities are lengths of intervals over (b−a).

sections.title: Worked: from PDF to probability
sections.setup: f(x)=2x on (0,1). Find P(X>0.5) and E[X].
sections.why: Continuous probabilities are areas under f. Expectation weights x by the density.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: For a continuous RV, P(X=3) is:
sections.explain: Points have probability zero under a continuous distribution; use intervals.

sections.title: Standardization
sections.body:
If X~N(μ,σ²), then Z=(X−μ)/σ ~ N(0,1).

P(X≤x)=P(Z≤(x−μ)/σ)=Φ((x−μ)/σ)

Use the exam normal table for Φ. For upper tails use symmetry: P(Z>z)=1−Φ(z), and Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z).

sections.title: Worked: standardize then table
sections.why: Every normal probability reduces to one standard normal probability. Memorize the standardize step so you never integrate the normal PDF by hand.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: If X~N(μ,σ²), then (X−μ)/σ is:
sections.explain: Standardization maps any normal to standard normal.

sections.title: Linear transforms & sums of independents
sections.body:
If X~N(μ,σ²) then aX+b ~ N(aμ+b, a²σ²).

If X,Y independent normals, then X+Y is normal with mean sum and variance sum.

Exam P rarely needs the full bivariate normal density; it does need standardize + table + variance of linear combos.

sections.title: Worked: between two values
sections.why: Always convert both endpoints to Z, then subtract CDFs. Sketch the bell if inequalities confuse you.

sections.title: Linear transform
sections.prompt: If X~N(2, 3²) then 4X+1 has variance:

sections.title: Exponential & memoryless
sections.body:
Watch parameterization:
• rate λ: f(x)=λe^{−λx}, E=1/λ, Var=1/λ²
• mean θ: f(x)=(1/θ)e^{−x/θ}, E=θ, Var=θ²

Memoryless: P(X>s+t|X>s)=P(X>t)
Survival: P(X>x)=e^{−x/θ} (mean form)

Min of independent Exp is Exp with summed rates.

sections.title: Gamma and Beta (exam level)
sections.body:
Gamma: flexible positive continuous family; exponential is Gamma with shape 1. Sums of i.i.d. Exp relate to Gamma/Erlang.

Beta: continuous on (0,1), useful for random proportions/probabilities.

You rarely need heavy MGF theory on current Exam P — focus on recognizing PDF, support, mean/variance when given, and computing integrals that are standard.

sections.title: Worked: memoryless
sections.setup: Waiting time ~ Exp(mean 10). Already waited 5. P(total wait > 12)?
sections.why: Memoryless says the past wait does not help; remaining time is still Exp(mean 10). Convert “total >12 given already 5” into “remaining >7”.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Which family is memoryless (continuous)?
sections.explain: Continuous memoryless ⇔ exponential.

sections.title: Loss vs payment
sections.body:
X = ground-up loss (what happened).
Y = payment by insurer (what is paid) after modifications.

Ordinary deductible d:
Y = 0 if X≤d, else X−d   i.e. Y=(X−d)+

Policy limit u (maximum paid on ground-up with no deductible):
Y=min(X,u)

Coinsurance α (insurer pays fraction α of the loss after other mods):
multiply payment by α.

Inflation: often replace X by (1+r)X before applying deductible/limit — read the order in the problem carefully.

sections.title: Per loss vs per payment
sections.body:
Per loss: includes zeros when no payment is made.
Per payment: conditional on payment being positive (given X>d).

E[payment per payment] = E[Y | Y>0]
which is larger than E[Y] when zeros exist.

Exam stems are picky about this wording.

sections.title: Worked: deductible expected payment
sections.setup: X~Exp(mean 1000), ordinary deductible 200. Find E[payment per loss].
sections.solution:
For exponential mean θ, E[(X−d)+]=θ e^{−d/θ}.
Here θ=1000,d=200 → 1000 e^{−0.2}.
sections.why: Memoryless/exponential tail formulas turn insurance modifications into quick closed forms. For other distributions, integrate survival: E[(X−d)+]=∫_d^∞ S(x)dx (when X≥0).

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: With ordinary deductible d, insurer payment per loss is:
sections.explain: Pays nothing below d, and the excess above d otherwise.

sections.title: Joint PMF
sections.body:
For discrete (X,Y):
 p(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y)
ΣΣ p(x,y)=1

Marginal of X: pX(x)=Σ_y p(x,y)
Conditional: p(y|x)=p(x,y)/pX(x)

Independent iff p(x,y)=pX(x)pY(y) for all x,y.

sections.title: Worked: marginal from a table
sections.why: Marginals collapse the joint by summing the other variable. Conditionals renormalize a slice of the joint table.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: Independence of discrete X,Y means:
sections.explain: Factorization of the joint PMF is the definition.

sections.title: Continuous joint densities
sections.body:
Joint PDF f(x,y) ≥ 0 with ∬ f=1.
Marginal fX(x)=∫ f(x,y) dy.
Conditional f(y|x)=f(x,y)/fX(x).
Independent iff f(x,y)=fX(x)fY(y) on a rectangle support (careful with non-rectangle supports — dependence can hide in the region).

sections.title: Worked: independence via factorization
sections.setup: f(x,y)=2 on 0<x<y<1 (and 0 else). Are X,Y independent?
sections.solution:
Support is a triangle, not a product rectangle ⇒ not independent.
(You can also check f ≠ fX fY.)
sections.why: Support shape alone can kill independence even if the formula 'looks separable' on the triangle.

sections.title: Marginal continuous
sections.prompt: Continuous marginal fX(x) is obtained by:
sections.explain: Integrate out the other variable.

sections.title: Cov and Corr
sections.body:
Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]
Corr(X,Y)=Cov(X,Y)/(SD(X)SD(Y)) ∈ [−1,1]

Var(aX+bY)=a²VarX+b²VarY+2ab Cov(X,Y)
If independent, Cov=0 (converse not always true in general, but exam often uses independence ⇒ Cov 0).

sections.title: Worked: variance of a sum
sections.setup: Independent X,Y with VarX=4, VarY=9. Find SD(X−2Y).
sections.why: Independence drops the covariance term. Coefficients square when they leave the variance.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: If X,Y independent, Var(X+Y) equals:
sections.explain: Independence ⇒ covariance 0 ⇒ variances add.

sections.title: E[XY] and bilinearity
sections.body:
E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y] always.
Cov is bilinear and symmetric; Cov(X,X)=Var(X).
Cov(X,c)=0 for constant c.

For uncorrelated variables Cov=0, Var(X+Y)=VarX+VarY.
Independence ⇒ uncorrelated; uncorrelated ⇏ independent in general.

sections.title: Worked: correlation from cov
sections.setup: VarX=4, VarY=9, Cov(X,Y)=3. Find Corr(X,Y).
sections.why: Divide by product of SDs, not variances.

sections.title: Var of linear combo
sections.prompt: Var(2X−3Y) expands to:
sections.explain: a=2,b=−3 ⇒ a²VarX+b²VarY+2ab Cov=4VarX+9VarY−12Cov.

sections.title: Order statistics (i.i.d.)
sections.body:
For i.i.d. continuous X1..Xn with CDF F:
Max Mn=X(n): P(Mn≤x)=[F(x)]^n
Min m=X(1): P(m>x)=[1−F(x)]^n , so P(m≤x)=1−[1−F(x)]^n

These show up with “largest claim”, “first arrival”, “weakest component”.

sections.title: CLT
sections.body:
For i.i.d. X_i with mean μ and variance σ² (finite),
S_n=X1+…+Xn ,  X̄=S_n/n

S_n ≈ Normal(nμ, nσ²)
X̄ ≈ Normal(μ, σ²/n)

Standardize:
P(X̄ ≤ a) ≈ Φ( (a−μ)/(σ/√n) )

sections.title: Worked: CLT for a mean
sections.setup: Claims have mean 200, SD 40. n=100 independent. Approx P(X̄>208).
sections.why: CLT turns a sum/mean of many i.i.d. variables into a normal probability, which we already know how to standardize.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: As n grows, Var(X̄) for i.i.d. finite-variance Xi:
sections.explain: Averaging reduces variance by factor n.

sections.title: How to review this week
sections.body:
No new Finan chapters. Loop:
1) Timed questions
2) Tag every miss by LO
3) Micro-drill only those LOs
4) Sleep

Use Wrong Pool + formula sheet. If stuck >2 minutes on a concept, Ask Grok, then re-try a similar problem immediately.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: In the final week, the best use of time is:
sections.explain: Mocks and diagnosis raise scores; new theory does not stabilize under time pressure.

sections.title: High-yield LO triage
sections.body:
Spend final-week time proportional to syllabus weight:
• Univariate (incl. insurance payments) — largest
• General conditionals/Bayes — frequent traps
• Multivariate joint/cov/CLT — fewer items but easy points if drilled

Keep a one-page formula sheet you can rewrite from memory in 10 minutes.

sections.title: Worked: 3-hour mock diagnosis loop
sections.setup: You score 18/30 on a mock. How to spend the next day?
sections.solution:
Tag each miss: setup error / formula / arithmetic / misread.
If ≥5 misses share a tag (e.g. deductible), do a 20-question micro-set only on that tag, then re-test 10 mixed.
sections.why: Random re-reading is comfort; tagged micro-drills change the score.

sections.title: v
sections.prompt: v equals:
sections.explain: Discount factor.

sections.title: Quick sheet
sections.body: a-angle-n=(1−v^n)/i ; ä-angle-n=(1−v^n)/d ; s-angle-n=((1+i)^n−1)/i.

sections.title: Perpetuity immediate
sections.prompt: PV of 1 per year forever (immediate) is:
sections.explain: Perpetuity-immediate 1/i.

transition.title: After Exam P: shift to FM

sections.title: How to pivot
sections.body:
If you passed P: make FM primary. Rebuild TVM fluency with BA II Plus, then annuities, loans, bonds, duration/immunization.

If not: rest a few days, then a 4-week P repair plan on Wrong Pool themes before heavy FM.

sections.title: Concept check
sections.prompt: After sitting P, the next priority if you passed is:

choices.B: Shift primary study to FM foundations

sections.explain: Your plan was P-first then FM primary after the sitting.

sections.title: What FM tests
sections.body:
Exam FM is a 2.5-hour, 30-question CBT on financial mathematics.

Approximate syllabus weights (use midpoints for planning):
• Time value of money ~10% (i, v, d, δ, nominal rates)
• Annuities ~25% (level, due/immediate, m-thly, continuous, varying)
• Loans ~20% (amortization, sinking funds)
• Bonds ~20% (price, book value, callable/redemption)
• General cash flows / portfolios / duration & immunization ~25%

Speed with a financial calculator (BA II Plus / TI-30X) is part of the skill.

sections.title: How this course is structured
sections.body:
Duolingo-style path:
Level 1 Learn → Level 2 Practice → Level 3 Drill → Chapter test (≥70%).
Last two weeks: wrap + full mocks only.
Do multiple levels per day if you want — soft goal is not a cap.

sections.title: Worked: exam mindset
sections.setup: A stem mixes nominal i^(2) with an annuity-due. What is the first move?
sections.solution: Convert everything to one consistent rate period (or use the matching symbol formula). Never mix end-of-year a-angle-n at effective i with half-year coupons without converting.
sections.why: Most FM errors are period mismatch, not hard algebra.

sections.title: Weight check
sections.prompt: Which block is usually the largest single topic group?
sections.explain: Annuities are typically the biggest pure block; portfolios/duration are also large.

fm_tvm_core.title: Interest measures: i, v, d, δ, nominal rates

sections.title: Core identities
sections.body:
Effective annual rate i: money multiplies by (1+i) per year.
Discount factor v = 1/(1+i).
Discount rate d = i/(1+i) = 1 − v.
Also i = d/(1−d).
Constant force of interest: δ = ln(1+i), accumulation a(t)=e^{δt}, v^t = e^{−δt}.

Nominal rates: i^{(m)} is payable m-thly; (1+i)=(1+i^{(m)}/m)^m.
Similarly (1−d)=(1−d^{(m)}/m)^m.

sections.title: Equivalent rates checklist
sections.body:
Given any one of i, v, d, δ, i^{(m)}, d^{(m)}, you should convert to any other in under 30 seconds.
Write the chain: i ↔ v ↔ d ↔ δ and i ↔ i^{(m)}.
On calculator: store i, compute v=1/(1+i), d=i/(1+i), δ=ln(1+i).

sections.title: Worked: force from effective
sections.setup: i = 0.06 effective annual. Find δ and d.
sections.why: Always sanity-check: 0 < d < i < δ is false actually — for positive rates, d < i and δ is between them in a specific way; just verify identities.

sections.title: Worked: nominal to effective
sections.setup: i^{(12)} = 0.12. Find effective annual i.
sections.why: Nominal 12% is not 12% effective — convert before multi-year problems.

sections.title: Identity
sections.prompt: Which is always true (positive i)?

fm_accum.title: Accumulation & present value of single payments

sections.title: Moving one payment
sections.body:
Future value: FV = PV · (1+i)^n   or   PV · e^{δn}.
Present value: PV = FV · v^n.
n can be fractional if compounding is continuous or if you use consistent period rate.
With nominal i^{(m)}, work in m-ths: period rate j=i^{(m)}/m, periods = m·t.

sections.title: Worked: two accounts meet
sections.setup: Classic: one account at nominal convertible m-thly, another at force δ; equal values after t years — solve for unknown rate.
sections.solution: Set AV1=AV2 ⇒ equate (1+j)^{mt} with e^{δt} (or the other accumulation function). Take logs / roots carefully.
sections.why: This is pure TVM algebra — define accumulation functions first.

sections.title: Worked: fractional year
sections.setup: 100 grows for 7.25 years at 4% convertible semiannually.
sections.solution: j=0.02 per half-year; k=14.5 periods; AV=100(1.02)^{14.5}.
sections.why: Count compounding periods, not calendar years with the wrong rate.

sections.title: PV factor
sections.prompt: At effective i, PV of 1 due in n years is:
sections.explain: Discount with v^n.

sections.title: Standard annual symbols
sections.body:
Annuity-immediate (payments of 1 at end of each year for n years):
  a-angle-n = (1 − v^n) / i
Annuity-due (payments at beginning of each year):
  ä-angle-n = (1 − v^n) / d = (1+i) a-angle-n
Accumulation of annuity-immediate: s-angle-n = (1+i)^n a-angle-n = ((1+i)^n − 1)/i
Due accumulation: s̈-angle-n = (1+i) s-angle-n
Perpetuity-immediate: 1/i ; due: 1/d.

sections.title: Payment level X
sections.body:
If payments are X (not 1), multiply the annuity factor by X.
PV = X · a-angle-n  (immediate) or X · ä-angle-n (due).
First identify timing: end vs beginning of periods.

sections.title: Worked: level payment PV
sections.setup: 500 at end of each year for 10 years, i=6%. PV?
sections.why: Factor out payment size; use immediate form for end-of-year.

sections.title: Worked: due vs immediate
sections.setup: Same payments as above but at the beginning of each year.
sections.why: Due is one period earlier ⇒ multiply immediate PV by (1+i).

sections.title: Due identity
sections.prompt: ä-angle-n equals:
sections.explain: Standard relationship.

sections.title: Payable m-thly
sections.body:
Level payments totaling 1 per year, paid m times per year (1/m each):
  a-angle-n^{(m)} = (1 − v^n) / i^{(m)}
Due form uses d^{(m)} in the denominator.
Continuous: ā-angle-n = (1 − v^n) / δ
More frequent payments (same annual total) raise PV slightly vs annual immediate.

sections.title: Calculator approach
sections.body:
Alternatively convert to period rate j and do an mn-payment annuity of 1/m each period.
Be consistent: either use m-thly symbols or expand to period form — not both mixed.

sections.title: Worked: monthly payments
sections.setup: Pay 1000 per year monthly for 20 years, i=5% effective. PV?
sections.why: Annual total 1000, paid monthly ⇒ m-thly annuity factor.

sections.title: Continuous denom
sections.prompt: Continuous annuity PV of rate 1 for n years uses denominator:
sections.explain: ā-angle-n = (1−v^n)/δ.

sections.title: Arithmetic patterns
sections.body:
Payments 1,2,...,n at year ends (immediate):
  (Ia)-angle-n = (ä-angle-n − n v^n) / i
Decreasing n,...,1:
  (Da)-angle-n = (n − a-angle-n) / i
There are due and continuous analogues — match the payment timing in the stem.

sections.title: Geometric growth
sections.body:
Payments grow by factor (1+g) each period.
Use adjusted rate j with 1+j = (1+i)/(1+g), then PV = first payment × a-angle-n at rate j
(with care at the first payment timing).
If g=i, special formulas (n v for certain perpetuity/level cases).

sections.title: Worked: increasing annuity
sections.setup: Payments 1,2,...,10 at year-end, interest i. PV?
sections.why: Don't sum 10 separate PVs unless n is tiny — use the closed form.

sections.title: Geometric idea
sections.prompt: Payments grow at g, interest i. Adjusted rate uses:
sections.explain: Standard substitution 1+j=(1+i)/(1+g).

sections.title: Level payment loan
sections.body:
Loan principal L repaid by n level payments X:
  L = X · a-angle-n  ⇒  X = L / a-angle-n
Outstanding balance after k payments (prospective):
  OB_k = X · a-angle-(n−k)
Retrospective:
  OB_k = L(1+i)^k − X · s-angle-k
Interest portion of payment k: I_k = i · OB_{k−1}
Principal portion: P_k = X − I_k

sections.title: Drop payments & refinancing
sections.body:
If a payment is missed or extra principal is paid, recompute OB then re-amortize remaining term or new payment.
Prospective method is usually cleanest after a change.

sections.title: Worked: find level payment
sections.setup: Loan 10,000 for 5 years, i=6% annual, level end-of-year payments.
sections.why: Always start from L = X a-angle-n unless the stem says otherwise.

sections.title: Worked: interest in a payment
sections.setup: After finding X and OB_2, interest in 3rd payment is i·OB_2.
sections.solution: I_3 = i · OB_2; principal = X − I_3.
sections.why: Interest is always rate times prior balance.

sections.title: Prospective OB
sections.prompt: After k level payments on an n-payment loan, OB equals X times:
sections.explain: Remaining annuity of n−k payments.

sections.title: Interest + sink
sections.body:
Borrower pays interest each period on the full principal L at loan rate i,
plus deposits into a sinking fund that accumulates to L at maturity at SF rate j.
Level SF deposit D = L / s-angle-n @ j.
Total periodic outlay = L·i + D  (if interest paid currently on full L).
If j ≠ i, only the SF uses j; interest leg uses i.

sections.title: Worked: total payment
sections.setup: L=1000, n=10, loan interest 8%, SF earns 6%. Annual total payment?
sections.solution:
Interest leg = 1000·0.08=80.
D = 1000 / s-angle-10 @ 6%.
Total = 80 + D.
sections.why: Two rates ⇒ two calculations.

sections.title: SF deposit
sections.prompt: To accumulate L in n periods at rate j in a sinking fund, level deposit is:
sections.explain: Future-value annuity accumulates deposits to L.

fm_bonds.title: Bond price, premium, discount, book value

sections.title: Price formula
sections.body:
Bond: face F, redemption C, n coupon periods, coupon rate r per period on F (coupon Fr),
yield rate i per coupon period:
  P = Fr · a-angle-n + C v^n
If coupons m-thly and yields nominal, convert to matching period rates first.
P > C ⇒ premium; P < C ⇒ discount; P = C ⇒ par (when coupon rate equals yield, C=F typically).

sections.title: Book value amortization
sections.body:
Book value just after a coupon follows the prospective formula with remaining coupons,
or recursive: BV_k = BV_{k−1}(1+i) − coupon.
Premium/discount write-down is |coupon − i·BV|.

sections.title: Worked: basic price
sections.setup: Face 1000, 10 years, 5% annual coupons, yield 6%, redeem at par.
sections.why: Coupon = 0.05·1000=50; redemption C=1000.

sections.title: Worked: premium vs discount
sections.setup: Same bond if yield is 4% instead of 6%.
sections.solution: Lower yield ⇒ higher price ⇒ premium bond (P>1000).
sections.why: Price and yield move inversely.

sections.title: Premium
sections.prompt: A bond sells at a premium when:
sections.explain: Premium means market price above redemption amount.

sections.title: Macaulay & modified duration
sections.body:
Macaulay duration MacD = weighted average payment time using PV weights of each cash flow.
For a level-yield i per period: ModD = MacD / (1+i).
Relative price change: ΔP/P ≈ −ModD · Δi  (first order).
Convexity adds a positive second-order term — prices rise more / fall less than duration alone predicts.

sections.title: Redington immunization
sections.body:
To immunize a liability:
1) PV(assets) = PV(liabilities)
2) MacD or ModD match (same derivative w.r.t. i)
3) Convexity of assets ≥ convexity of liabilities
Assumes small parallel yield shifts and cash flows fixed.

sections.title: Worked: duration intuition
sections.setup: Zero-coupon bond maturing in n years has MacD = n.
sections.solution: All weight sits at time n ⇒ MacD=n. Coupon bonds have MacD < maturity.
sections.why: More coupons earlier ⇒ shorter duration.

sections.title: Price sensitivity
sections.prompt: If yields rise slightly, bond prices:
sections.explain: dP/P ≈ −ModD·Δi.

sections.title: Cold formula gate
sections.body:
Before mocks, rewrite from memory:
• i,v,d,δ and nominal conversions
• a, ä, s, s̈, a^{(m)}, ā, (Ia), (Da)
• Loan OB prospective/retrospective + I_k, P_k
• Bond price + book value recursion
• MacD, ModD, Redington conditions

sections.title: Mock loop
sections.body:
Full 30Q / 2.5h → tag misses (period mismatch / formula / calculator) → micro-drill → re-mock.
No new theory in the final two weeks.

sections.title: Final weeks
sections.prompt: Best use of the last two weeks:

choices.B: Timed mixed sets + full mocks + wrong pool

sections.explain: Wrap unit is mock-heavy by design.

sections.title: What FAM is
sections.body:
Exam FAM (Fundamentals of Actuarial Mathematics) is a 3.5-hour CBT with ~34 multiple-choice questions.

It blends:
• Short-term: severity/frequency/aggregate, policy mods, intro estimation & credibility
• Long-term: survival models, life insurance & annuities, premiums & reserves

Prerequisites: Exam P (probability), FM (financial math), and VEE mathematical statistics ideas.
Tables (life/decrement and distribution inventories) are provided in the exam environment.

sections.title: How this course runs
sections.body:
Duolingo path: Learn → Practice → Drill → Chapter test (≥70%).
Rough study split follows weights: ST block first, then LT (larger share of exam time for many sittings),
then wrap with mixed mocks. Multi-level days are allowed.

sections.title: Structure
sections.prompt: FAM content is best studied as:
sections.explain: Official FAM spans short-term and long-term foundations.

sections.title: Severity building blocks
sections.body:
Severity = size of loss (given a loss occurs).
Common families: exponential, gamma, Pareto, lognormal, Weibull (use provided tables on exam).
Know mean, variance, limited expected value e(d)=E[X∧d], and mean excess e_X(d)=E[X−d|X>d].
For positive continuous X: E[X] = ∫_0^∞ S(x) dx (when finite).

sections.title: Limited loss & excess
sections.body:
E[X∧u] is expected payment with limit u (no deductible).
With ordinary deductible d and max payment u−d (limit u ground-up):
E[payment] = E[X∧u] − E[X∧d]  (common identity).
Mean excess for memoryless exponential equals mean — classic trap check.

sections.title: Worked: exponential deductible
sections.setup: X ~ Exp(mean θ=1000). Ordinary deductible 200. E[payment per loss]?
sections.why: Exponential memoryless turns excess problems into survival × mean.

sections.title: Limited expected value use
sections.prompt: E[X∧u] is most directly the expected:

choices.A: Payment with ordinary deductible u only
choices.B: Loss capped at u (policy limit, no deductible)

sections.explain: Limited expected value caps the ground-up loss at u.

sections.title: Modifications
sections.body:
Deductible, limit, coinsurance α: payment often α·min(max(X−d,0), u−d).
Per-payment vs per-loss: conditioning on X>d changes the distribution of payment.
Inflation: scale severity, then re-apply mods (order matters).

sections.title: Risk measures (intro)
sections.body:
VaR_p(X) = F^{-1}(p) (quantile).
TVaR_p(X) = E[X | X > VaR_p] (or integral form of tail expectation).
Know qualitative: TVaR ≥ VaR; coherence properties at a high level.

sections.title: Coinsurance
sections.prompt: With coinsurance α∈(0,1) and no other mods, insurer payment is:
sections.explain: Insurer pays fraction α of the loss (as worded).

sections.title: Limited fluctuation (classical)
sections.body:
Choose n so the sample mean is within k of μ with probability p (standard normal approximation).
Full credibility standard n0; partial credibility Z=√(n/n0) (capped at 1) in classical approach.

sections.title: Bühlmann credibility
sections.body:
Z = n / (n+K), K = EVPV / VHM
(expected process variance / variance of hypothetical means).
Estimate = Z·X̄ + (1−Z)·prior mean (manual/complementary).
As n→∞, Z→1.

sections.title: Worked: Bühlmann Z
sections.setup: n=20, K=30. Find Z.
sections.why: More data or smaller K ⇒ higher credibility.

sections.title: Bühlmann Z limit
sections.prompt: As n→∞, Bühlmann Z approaches:
sections.explain: Full weight on the observed mean.

sections.title: Lifetime random variables
sections.body:
T_x = future lifetime of (x).
Survival: _t p_x = P(T_x > t)
Death: _t q_x = 1 − _t p_x
Deferred: _t|u q_x = _t p_x · _u q_{x+t}
Force of mortality μ_{x+t}; relationships with survival function.
Curate K_x = ⌊T_x⌋ for discrete models.

sections.title: Life table functions
sections.body:
l_x, d_x = l_x − l_{x+1}, q_x = d_x/l_x, p_x = 1−q_x.
e_x = curtate expectation of future lifetime (sum of p's).
Under UDD or constant force, convert between continuous and discrete probabilities.

sections.title: Worked: two-year survival
sections.why: Chain single-year survivals for multi-year.

sections.title: Notation
sections.prompt: _t p_x is the probability that (x):
sections.explain: p is survival; q is death.

sections.title: Insurance EPV
sections.body:
Whole life insurance pays 1 at end of year of death: A_x = Σ v^{k+1} · _k|q_x
Continuous whole life Ā_x integrates v^t · _t p_x μ_{x+t} dt.
Term, pure endowment A_{x:n|}^1 , endowment insurance A_{x:n|}.
Identity (discrete whole life, level i): A_x = 1 − d ä_x.

sections.title: Relations
sections.body:
Pure endowment: A_{x:n|}^{1|} = v^n · _n p_x
Endowment insurance = term insurance + pure endowment.
Higher interest rate lowers insurance APVs (discount harder).

sections.title: Worked: identity
sections.setup: Given ä_x and d, find A_x for whole life discrete.
sections.why: Memorize this identity cold.

sections.title: Insurance vs annuity
sections.prompt: A_x = 1 − d ä_x links:

choices.B: Whole life insurance to life annuity-due

sections.explain: Classic discrete whole-life identity.

sections.title: Prospective reserve
sections.body:
Net premium reserve at duration t:
  _t V = EPV future benefits − EPV future net premiums
(conditional on survival to t, using select/ultimate as given).
At issue, _0 V = 0 under equivalence.
Retrospective: accumulated past premiums − accumulated past benefits (with interest/survivorship).

sections.title: Whole life formula
Worked: prospective idea
sections.setup: After t years, future benefit APV is 0.4, future premium annuity APV is 8, net P=0.03.
sections.why: Prospective: future benefits minus future premiums.

sections.title: Issue reserve
sections.prompt: Under equivalence net premium, issue reserve is typically:
sections.explain: EPV premiums = EPV benefits at issue ⇒ reserve 0.

sections.title: Two-track review
sections.body:
Split practice days: ST (severity/aggregate/credibility) vs LT (A_x, ä_x, P, V).
Then mixed timed sets. Use exam tables in practice if you have them.
Formula sheet: compound variance, Bühlmann Z, A=1−dä, P=A/ä, prospective V.

sections.title: Mix
sections.prompt: A good FAM wrap week includes:

choices.C: Both ST and LT timed mixes

sections.explain: The exam mixes both domains.

sections.title: What SRM covers
sections.body:
Statistics for Risk Modeling: supervised learning, GLMs, time series, PCA/clustering, tree-based models.
You need conceptual fluency + interpretation of model output, not production ML engineering.

sections.title: Not the focus
sections.prompt: SRM is least about:
sections.explain: It is a modeling/statistics exam, not devops.

sections.title: Train / validation / test
sections.body:
Split data to estimate generalization.
Bias–variance tradeoff: flexible models can overfit.
Cross-validation estimates out-of-sample error.
Feature engineering and leakage awareness matter.

sections.title: Overfitting
sections.prompt: Overfitting typically means:
sections.explain: Memorizing training noise fails on new data.

srm_glm.title: GLMs for count & severity style responses

sections.title: GLM structure
sections.body:
Random component (exponential family), linear predictor η=Xβ, link g(μ)=η.
Log link for positive means; logit for probabilities.
Coefficients: for log link, e^{β} is a multiplicative effect.
Offset terms appear with exposure.

sections.title: Log link
sections.prompt: With log link, a coefficient β=0.2 roughly multiplies mean by:
sections.explain: μ ∝ e^{Xβ}; unit increase multiplies by e^β.

sections.title: Trend, seasonality, noise
sections.body:
Decompose series; stationary vs nonstationary.
AR, MA, ARIMA intuition: lags of series and shocks.
ACF/PACF patterns guide orders (conceptually).
Forecast intervals widen with horizon.

sections.title: Stationarity
sections.prompt: A stationary series has roughly stable:
sections.explain: Classical stationarity assumptions target stable moments/dependence.

sections.title: Unsupervised tools
sections.body:
PCA: orthogonal directions of maximum variance; use for dimension reduction.
Clustering (k-means, hierarchical): group similar observations; choose k with care.
Scale features before distance-based methods.

sections.title: PCA goal
sections.prompt: First principal component captures:
sections.explain: PC1 maximizes variance among unit linear combinations.

sections.title: Tree family
sections.body:
Decision trees partition feature space; easy to overfit if deep.
Bagging/RF: average many trees, reduce variance; RF also randomizes features.
Boosting: sequential focus on residuals/errors; strong predictive performance, less interpretable.

sections.title: RF idea
sections.prompt: Random forests mainly reduce error by:
sections.explain: Ensemble averaging + feature randomness.

sections.title: Interpretation first
sections.body: On exam day, read the stem for the modeling goal, metric, and pitfall (leakage, imbalance, overfitting).

sections.title: Priority
sections.prompt: When a stem gives GLM coefficients with log link, first translate to:
sections.explain: Interpretation is the SRM skill.

sections.title: Project mindset
sections.body:
Predictive Analytics is a structured written/project-style assessment:
problem statement → data/EDA → modeling → communication.
Grading rewards clear business framing and justified model choices, not only accuracy.

sections.title: Communication
sections.prompt: PA success requires:
sections.explain: Communication is explicitly weighted.

sections.title: Define the decision
sections.body:
Translate a business ask into a modeling target, population, time frame, and metric (loss, AUC, RMSE, lift).
State constraints: fairness, latency, interpretability, data freshness.

sections.title: Metric match
sections.prompt: Class imbalance often makes raw accuracy:
sections.explain: Prefer precision/recall/AUC/log-loss as appropriate.

sections.title: Look before you model
sections.body:
Missingness patterns, outliers, leakage, target leakage from future fields, leakage via IDs.
Plots: distributions, relationships, time drift.
Document cleaning rules so results are reproducible.

sections.title: Leakage
sections.prompt: Using a feature only known after the claim is closed is often:
sections.explain: Training on future information invents fake performance.

sections.title: Compare honestly
sections.body:
Baselines first. Then GLM / trees / others as appropriate.
Validate with proper splits or time-based splits for temporal data.
Tune complexity with CV; report uncertainty and error analysis.

sections.prompt: A simple baseline model is useful because:

choices.B: It anchors whether complexity is worth it

sections.explain: Always beat a sane baseline.

Lead with the recommendation, then evidence.
Limitations, monitoring plan, and next data collection step.
Exhibits should be labeled for a non-ML manager.

sections.explain: Decision-oriented communication.

Pure premium, loss ratio methods, exposure bases, classification relativities, trend and development.

choices.B: Incurred but not reported (and related) liabilities

Quota share, surplus, excess of loss, stop-loss — who pays which layer.
Effect on net severity/frequency and capital.

sections.title: Core object
sections.prompt: Long-term models center on:
sections.explain: Life-contingent payments over decades.

sections.body:
Healthy/disabled/dead states; transition intensities.
Multiple decrement tables; associated single decrement rates.
Careful with timing assumptions.

sections.prompt: A disability model typically needs:

choices.C: Only one cash flow at t=0

sections.explain: States + transitions drive contingent benefits.

sections.title: Design levers
sections.body:
Term, whole life, endowments, annuities, riders.
Profit testing: best-estimate assumptions, risk discount rate, surplus emerging.
Sensitivities: mortality, lapse, expense, interest.

sections.title: Lapse risk
sections.prompt: Higher lapses can hurt products that:

choices.B: Rely on long persistency to recover acquisition costs

sections.explain: Acquisition cost recovery needs persistency.

sections.body:
Net premium vs modified reserves; expense loads.
Regulatory vs economic views (high level).
Connect to FAM reserve basics; add product-level detail.

sections.title: Issue reserve
sections.prompt: Under equivalence net premium, issue reserve is typically:
sections.explain: Equivalence sets EPV premiums = EPV benefits at issue.

sections.title: Drill
sections.body: Mixed life-contingency calculations + short written interpretation of profit test output.

sections.title: Balance
sections.prompt: LT wrap should include:
sections.explain: Matches the track.

sections.title: Coverage language
sections.body:
Short-term coverages pay benefits over a short policy period (often one year).
Key ideas: ground-up loss vs payment, per-loss vs per-payment, ordinary deductible, franchise,
policy limit, coinsurance, maximum covered loss.
Reinsurance layers (quota share, excess of loss) shift which portion of losses the insurer retains.

sections.title: Worked: ordinary deductible payment
sections.setup: Loss X. Ordinary deductible d. Insurer payment per loss?
sections.solution:
Y = max(X − d, 0)  (also written (X−d)+).
If a policy limit u applies to ground-up, payment is min(max(X−d,0), u−d) depending on wording — read carefully.
sections.why: Always define the payment random variable before computing E[Y] or F_Y.

sections.title: Ordinary deductible
sections.prompt: With ordinary deductible d, insurer payment per loss is:
sections.explain: Ordinary deductible pays the excess over d.

sections.title: Frequency
sections.body:
N = claim count. Common models: Poisson(λ), binomial(m,q), negative binomial.
Poisson: E[N]=Var(N)=λ.
NB has variance > mean (overdispersion vs Poisson).

sections.title: Aggregate S
sections.body:
Collective risk: S = X1+···+XN with Xi iid severity, independent of N (usual assumption).
E[S] = E[N] E[X]
Var(S) = E[N] Var(X) + Var(N) (E[X])²
Compound Poisson is especially tractable; (a,b,0) class recursions appear at intro level.

sections.title: Worked: mean and variance of S
sections.setup: N~Poisson(3), X has E[X]=100, Var(X)=400, independent.
sections.why: Plug into the compound variance formula; don't forget the Var(N)(EX)² term.

sections.title: Aggregate mean
sections.prompt: If N ⊥ X_i iid, E[S] equals:
sections.explain: Wald identity for random sums.

sections.title: MLE / method of moments ideas
sections.body:
Fit a parametric severity/frequency by matching sample moments or maximizing likelihood.
For exponential, MLE of mean is sample mean.
Censoring/truncation (policy limits, deductibles) change the likelihood — write the correct contribution per observation.

sections.title: Worked: exponential MLE
sections.setup: Ground-up losses, Exp(θ), complete data x1..xn. Estimate θ=E[X].
sections.why: Complete i.i.d. exponential: MLE is the sample mean.

sections.title: Data type
sections.prompt: A policy limit typically creates:
sections.explain: You observe the limit, not the full ground-up amount.

sections.title: Annuity EPVs
sections.body:
Annuity-due ä_x : 1 per year while (x) alive, paid at beginning of year.
Annuity-immediate a_x : payments at end of year.
Temporary ä_{x:n|}, deferred _n|ä_x.
Continuous ā_x.
Relationships: ä_x = 1 + a_x  (under standard discrete timing).

sections.title: Worked: temporary due
sections.setup: Express ä_{x:n|} in terms of pure endowment and whole-life style sums.
sections.why: Finite sum of discounted survival probabilities.

sections.title: Due vs immediate
sections.prompt: Under standard annual models, ä_x equals:
sections.explain: Due pays one more certain first payment structure ⇒ 1+a_x.

sections.title: Net premiums
sections.body:
Equivalence: EPV(premiums) = EPV(benefits) at issue (ignore expenses for net premium).
Whole life level annual due: P_x = A_x / ä_x
Term, endowment have analogous ratios benefit APV / annuity APV.
Gross premiums add expense loading (percent of premium, per policy, per face).
